evals.name: interface-at-consumer-not-implementor
evals.description: Tests whether the model defines interfaces where they are consumed, not where they are implemented
evals.prompt: I'm writing a Go notification service that can send emails. I have an email package with a Client struct that has a Send method. I also have a notification package that needs to use this email client. Where should I define the interface?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model often puts the interface in the email package (the implementor). The skill says interfaces MUST be defined where consumed, not where implemented.
expectations: Interface is defined in the notification package (the consumer), NOT in the email package
Interface has only the methods the notification package needs (not the full email.Client API)
Email package exports a concrete Client struct, not an interface
Explains WHY: keeps the consumer in control of the contract, avoids importing a package just for its interface
Notification service depends on its own interface, not on email package types

evals.name: return-structs-not-interfaces
evals.description: Tests whether the model returns concrete types from constructors, not interfaces
evals.prompt: I'm designing a Go package with a UserService that depends on a UserStore interface. Should my NewUserService constructor return *UserService or UserServiceInterface? Show me the constructor signature.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may suggest returning an interface for 'flexibility' or 'abstraction'. The skill says functions SHOULD return concrete types -- NEVER return interfaces from constructors.
expectations: Constructor returns *UserService (concrete type), NOT an interface
Constructor accepts UserStore as an interface parameter (accept interfaces)
Explains WHY: callers get full access to the concrete type's fields/methods; consumers can assign to interface if needed
Explicitly states that returning interfaces from constructors is bad practice
The accept-interfaces-return-structs principle is stated or demonstrated

evals.name: premature-interface-trap
evals.description: Tests whether the model avoids creating interfaces prematurely when there is only one implementation
evals.prompt: I'm writing a Go application with a UserRepository that talks to PostgreSQL. It's the only database we'll ever use. Should I create a UserRepository interface and a concrete postgresUserRepository struct, or just use a concrete struct directly?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model almost always suggests creating an interface 'for testability' even with a single implementation. The skill says NEVER create interfaces prematurely -- wait for 2+ implementations or a testability requirement.
expectations: Recommends starting with a concrete struct (not an interface) when there is only one implementation
Mentions the principle: don't design with interfaces, discover them
Suggests extracting an interface LATER when a second consumer or test mock demands it
Acknowledges that testability IS a valid reason to add an interface, but it should be a deliberate choice
Does NOT reflexively recommend creating an interface just because it is a repository

evals.name: zero-value-useful-design
evals.description: Tests whether the model designs structs with useful zero values using lazy initialization
evals.prompt: I have a Go Registry struct that stores items in a map. Users are getting panics when they call Register without calling NewRegistry first. How should I fix this?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may just say 'always call the constructor' or add nil checks at every call site. The skill says to make the zero value useful with lazy initialization.
expectations: Recommends lazy initialization in the Register method (if r.items == nil { r.items = make(...) })
Mentions the Go principle: make the zero value useful
The fix allows using var r Registry without calling a constructor
Does NOT just say 'always use the constructor' as the primary fix
References bytes.Buffer or sync.Mutex as stdlib examples of useful zero values

evals.name: embedding-vs-named-field
evals.description: Tests whether the model correctly distinguishes when to embed vs use a named field
evals.prompt: I have a Go Server struct that uses a DataStore for persistence and an http.Handler for routing. Should I embed both, use named fields for both, or mix? The Server should expose the Handler's ServeHTTP method but should NOT expose DataStore's internal methods to callers.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may embed both or use named fields for both. The skill has a clear rule: embed when you want to promote the full API ('is a'), named field when you only need it internally ('has a').
expectations: Embeds http.Handler (to promote ServeHTTP to the Server)
Uses a named field for DataStore (not embedded, because its methods should not be exposed)
Explains the embed vs named field rule: embed for 'is a' (promote full API), named field for 'has a' (internal use)
Mentions that embedding promotes ALL methods of the inner type, which can be undesirable
Notes that the receiver of promoted methods is the inner type, not the outer type

evals.name: compile-time-interface-check
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses compile-time interface verification
evals.prompt: I have a Go type MyBuffer that should implement io.ReadWriter. How can I make sure the compiler catches it if I accidentally break the interface contract later?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may suggest writing a test or just relying on usage sites to catch it. The skill recommends the var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil) pattern.
expectations: Uses var _ io.ReadWriter = (*MyBuffer)(nil) pattern
Places the check near the type definition
Explains that this costs nothing at runtime
Explains that the build fails immediately if MyBuffer stops satisfying the interface

evals.name: type-assertion-comma-ok
evals.description: Bare type assertions panic on wrong type; comma-ok is required even when the type 'should always' be correct
evals.trap: The teammate's argument sounds reasonable — the caller controls event construction and should always set the correct payload type. But bare type assertions panic at runtime on any mismatch (future code, deserialized events, tests with wrong setup). The model should reject the teammate's argument and use comma-ok form.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's argument — bare type assertions panic at runtime on any type mismatch, regardless of how controlled the callers seem
Uses comma-ok form for all three type assertions: payload, ok := e.Payload.(*UserCreated)
Handles the !ok case by returning an error (not panicking) — e.g., 'unexpected payload type for user.created'
Explains the failure mode: future code, deserialized events from external sources, or tests with wrong fixture setup will cause unrecoverable panics with bare assertions

evals.name: optional-behavior-type-assertion
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses type assertions for optional interface capabilities
evals.prompt: I'm writing a Go function that writes data to an io.Writer. Some writers support flushing (like bufio.Writer) but not all. I want to flush after writing IF the writer supports it, but not require all writers to implement Flush. How should I design this?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may create a WriteAndFlusher interface and require all callers to implement it. The skill shows the optional behavior pattern with type assertion.
expectations: Defines a separate Flusher interface with just the Flush method
Function parameter is io.Writer (not a combined interface)
Uses type assertion (f, ok := w.(Flusher)) to check for flush capability
Only calls Flush if the type assertion succeeds
Mentions this pattern is used in the standard library (e.g. http.Flusher, io.ReaderFrom)

evals.name: nocopy-sentinel-struct
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses the noCopy sentinel to prevent struct copying
evals.prompt: I have a Go struct ConnPool that contains a sync.Mutex and a slice of connections. A junior developer accidentally passed it by value to a function, which caused a data race. How can I prevent this struct from being copied?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may just say 'always use pointers' or rely on code review. The skill shows the noCopy sentinel pattern that makes go vet catch accidental copies.
expectations: Recommends embedding a noCopy sentinel struct
noCopy implements Lock() and Unlock() methods (empty bodies)
Explains that go vet will flag copies of structs containing noCopy
Mentions this is the same technique used by sync.WaitGroup, sync.Mutex, or strings.Builder in the stdlib
Shows that the struct should be passed by pointer after adding noCopy

evals.name: generics-over-any-interface
evals.description: Tests whether the model prefers generics over any/interface{} for type-safe operations
evals.prompt: I need to write a Go function that checks if a slice contains a given element. The function should work with any comparable type (ints, strings, etc.). What's the best approach?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may use []any and any parameters for compatibility. The skill says MUST prefer generics over any for type-safe operations (Go 1.18+).
expectations: Uses generics with a type parameter: func Contains[T comparable](slice []T, target T) bool
Does NOT use []any or interface{} parameters
Uses the comparable constraint for the type parameter
Explains WHY: generics preserve type safety, while any loses it
Mentions that any should only be used at true boundaries where type is genuinely unknown (JSON decoding, reflection)

evals.name: receiver-consistency-rule
evals.description: Tests whether the model enforces consistent receiver types across all methods of a type
evals.prompt: I have a Go struct with 5 methods. Four use value receivers and one uses a pointer receiver because it modifies the struct. Is this fine?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model may accept the mixed receiver approach as valid for each method. The skill says receiver type MUST be consistent -- if one method uses pointer, all should.
expectations: Says mixing pointer and value receivers on the same type is wrong or not recommended
Recommends making ALL methods use pointer receivers since one needs to mutate
Explains WHY: consistency rule -- if any method uses a pointer receiver, all should
Mentions that method sets differ for T and *T which affects interface satisfaction
